cases.case_name: In re Adoption/Guardianship of Rashawn H.
cases.holding: Reversing a termination of parental rights, the Court held that a juvenile court may terminate parental rights only if it finds, by clear and convincing evidence and with findings tied to the statutory factors, that the parent is unfit to continue the parental relationship or that exceptional circumstances make continuing it detrimental to the child's best interest.
cases.quote: the kind of unfitness or exceptional circumstances necessary to rebut the substantive presumption must be established by clear and convincing evidence, not by the mere preponderance standard

relevance.OUT-02: Rashawn H. is Maryland's controlling statement of the TPR substantive standard and burden of proof that governs every termination decision.
relevance.DEC-03: The Court's insistence that findings be tied to statutory criteria and proved to a heightened standard frames how agency findings must later be proved in court.
relevance.ACT-02: The opinion explains that the same statutory factors that measure the department's services also measure unfitness, so court-ordered service plans are the evidentiary record for later TPR.

cases.holding: The Court reversed permanency-plan orders after holding that a permanency plan decision is reviewed overall for abuse of discretion while the underlying factual findings are reviewed for clear error, and that the findings there were unsupported by competent evidence.
cases.quote: The appellate standard of review as to the overall determination of the hearing court is one of "abuse of discretion."

relevance.ACT-03: Yve S. supplies the standard by which a foster-care/permanency placement order is reviewed on appeal.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading Maryland statement of when an appellate court may reverse a juvenile court's child-welfare decision.
relevance.PMC-06: Its three-tier review framework is the analytic template for auditing whether a juvenile court decision rests on supported findings.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption/Guardianship of Ta'Niya C.
cases.holding: Vacating a denial of termination, the Court clarified that Rashawn H. did not displace the best-interest standard: unfitness and exceptional circumstances are measured through, not apart from, the child's best interest, which remains the governing standard in TPR cases.
cases.quote: we reexamine the law in this area and confirm once again that the child's best interest is the prevailing standard in these determinations

relevance.OUT-02: Ta'Niya C. fixes the relationship between the parental presumption and the best-interest standard that decides every Maryland TPR case.
relevance.OUT-03: Because guardianship alternatives are judged by the same best-interest inquiry, this case governs the choice between TPR and a permanent third-party arrangement.
relevance.DEC-03: The opinion confirms that agency findings feed a best-interest analysis rather than a free-standing fault determination.

cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA's 'active efforts' requirement is satisfied by substantive proof that the department made, and exhausted, remedial and rehabilitative efforts, and that the juvenile court need not recite the statute's wording; it reversed the intermediate court and directed that the circuit court judgment be affirmed.
cases.quote: what is important is whether the Department in substance made active efforts to prevent the breakup of the family, whether those efforts were unsuccessful

relevance.INP-11: This is Maryland's only high-court decision applying the Indian Child Welfare Act in a CINA case and it defines what triggers and satisfies the federal standard.
relevance.ACT-02: It sets the content of the heightened 'active efforts' service obligation that displaces ordinary reasonable efforts for an Indian child.
relevance.OUT-01: It governs when a CINA case involving an Indian child may be closed without reunification.

cases.holding: The Court held that a sibling seeking visitation over a parent's objection is a third party who must make the Koshko threshold showing of parental unfitness or exceptional circumstances, and it remanded for consideration of jurisdiction and of deleterious effect on the siblings.
cases.quote: A person, thus, seeking visitation, who is not a biological or adoptive parent is a third party. A sibling, whether full, half or CINA, remains a third party.

relevance.ACT-04: It controls when a juvenile court may order contact between a child in care and kin or siblings living with a parent.
relevance.ACT-03: The opinion reads FL § 5-525.2 as reaching only siblings who are themselves in out-of-home placement, which limits sibling-placement and visitation orders in foster care.
relevance.OUT-03: It defines the third-party burden that a relative or sibling must carry when seeking court-ordered access as part of a permanency arrangement.

cases.case_name: Horridge v. St. Mary's County Department of Social Services
cases.holding: Reversing dismissal of a wrongful-death complaint, the Court held that FL § 5-706 and its regulations create a mandatory duty owed to the identified child named in an abuse report, so the public duty doctrine does not bar a negligence action against the department and its caseworkers.
cases.quote: This is not an obligation that runs to everyone in general and no one in particular. It runs to an identified or identifiable child or discrete group of children.

relevance.INP-01: It establishes that the statutory response duty triggered by a mandated report runs to the specific child named, not merely to the public.
relevance.INP-02: The same duty attaches to reports from any source, including a non-mandated relative such as the grandfather plaintiff here.
relevance.INP-03: It describes the joint department/law-enforcement investigation regime that a referral sets in motion.
relevance.INP-04: It catalogues the mandatory investigative steps a court-referred report obliges the department to take.
relevance.INP-05: The plaintiff here was a family member asking the agency for help, and the case defines what the agency then owes.
relevance.INP-06: Reports received by the department by telephone triggered the mandatory duties the Court enforced.
relevance.INP-07: The Court's description of § 5-706 duties governs the agency response to a health-care-generated report.
relevance.INP-08: Absent a Maryland case on educator reporting specifically, this decision supplies the duty owed once any mandated reporter's report is received.
relevance.INP-09: The decision is the principal Maryland vehicle for external accountability when systemic investigative failures come to light.
relevance.INP-10: It requires the department to clarify incomplete reports rather than screen them out, constraining escalation decisions.
relevance.DEC-02: It makes prompt on-site investigation of each accepted report a mandatory, non-discretionary duty.
relevance.DEC-05: It notes the department's obligation to petition the juvenile court when the child's protection requires it.
relevance.OUT-06: The case arose from a child beaten to death eight days after the last ignored report and defines agency liability for that outcome.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is Maryland's controlling authority on civil liability for a child's death after agency failure to investigate.
relevance.PMC-02: Judicial enforcement of § 5-706 duties is the accountability backstop where audit and oversight fail.
relevance.PMC-03: The Court's reasoning about a statutorily protected class of children is the doctrinal basis for external review of agency performance.
relevance.PMC-04: It is the leading Maryland fatality case articulating what the agency was required to do before the death.
relevance.PMC-06: Its duty analysis supplies the legal yardstick for flagging investigative failures in Maryland cases.
relevance.ACT-05: It notes the department's authority to seek commitment or custody, including protective relief, based on its findings.
relevance.ACT-06: The mandated investigation includes determining the child's condition and needed services, including medical care.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption/Guardianship of Alonza D.
cases.holding: The Court reversed termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights because the circuit court found 'exceptional circumstances' without making the explicit finding, required by Rashawn H., that a continued parental relationship would be detrimental to the children's best interests.
cases.quote: We conclude that the Circuit Court erred by failing to make explicit findings that a continued parental relationship would be detrimental to the best interests of the children

relevance.OUT-02: Alonza D. is Maryland's leading decision on terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent and the findings that must accompany it.
relevance.OUT-03: It shows that placing children with a caretaker short of termination requires the court to articulate why the parental tie itself is detrimental.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a paradigm reversal for failure to make the constitutionally required findings.

cases.holding: The Court held that purely custodial (Ross) factors have no place in a TPR analysis under FL § 5-323, but that the juvenile court's incidental reference to them did not taint findings otherwise properly made under the statute, so termination was affirmed.
cases.quote: Although factors pertaining exclusively to custody have no place in TPR assessments under FL § 5-323, the juvenile court did not abuse its discretion

relevance.OUT-02: H.W. confines the TPR inquiry to the statutory factors and forbids comparing the parent to the foster placement as if it were a custody contest.
relevance.ACT-03: It limits how a child's foster placement may be weighed against the parent when permanency decisions are made.
relevance.OUT-03: It marks the doctrinal line between third-party custody analysis and termination analysis.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Jayden G.
cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination, holding that whether to stay a TPR case while an appeal of a permanency-plan change is pending is committed to the juvenile court's discretion and that the court properly considered the child's attachment to his foster parents.
cases.quote: whether to stay a TPR case is within the juvenile court's discretion

relevance.OUT-02: It governs the sequencing of permanency-plan appeals and TPR proceedings, a recurring trap for parents' counsel.
relevance.ACT-03: The Court approved weighing a child's bond with a long-term foster placement in the permanency analysis.
relevance.ACT-04: The opinion addresses the department's exploration of a grandmother as a relative resource before the plan changed to non-relative adoption.
relevance.FAIL-01: It explains why a successful appeal of a plan change may come too late to undo a termination entered in the interim.

cases.holding: The Court held that a juvenile court may award custody under CJP § 3-819(e) only after sustaining the petition against one parent and finding the other able and willing to care for the child, that the best-interest standard governs the exercise of that discretion, and that the parent must be allowed an evidentiary hearing on material disputes.
cases.quote: If those prerequisites are established, the best interest of the child is the standard that applies to the court's decision whether and, if so, how to exercise that discretion

relevance.DEC-05: It defines the findings that must support a CINA petition before the court may reallocate custody instead of adjudicating the child CINA.
relevance.OUT-05: It governs the common disposition in which the CINA case is closed with a custody award to the non-offending parent.
relevance.INP-04: It describes the juvenile court's role in directing outcomes once a petition is before it.

cases.holding: Resolving a split in the intermediate court, the Court held that an order waiving the department's obligation to make reasonable reunification efforts is not immediately appealable under CJP § 12-303(3)(x) because, standing alone, it does not deprive the parent of care or custody.
cases.quote: juvenile court's order waiving a department's obligation to provide reasonable reunification efforts, while leaving a custody order and permanency plan unchanged, does not deprive a parent of care or custody

relevance.ACT-02: It fixes the procedural consequence of a § 3-812 waiver of court-ordered reunification services.
relevance.OUT-01: A reasonable-efforts waiver is the formal end of the reunification track, and this case says when it can be challenged.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the controlling authority on interlocutory appealability of agency-favorable CINA orders.
relevance.FAIL-03: Reasonable efforts are a Title IV-E funding condition, and this case governs judicial review of their waiver.
relevance.PMC-01: Judicial reasonable-efforts determinations are the data point CFSR reviews rely on, and this case controls their reviewability.

cases.holding: The Court held that a juvenile court abuses its discretion when it declines to terminate parental rights and instead leaves the child indefinitely in third-party custody after finding that neither parent can ever safely care for the child.
cases.quote: The finding that Father was not unfit is contradicted by the juvenile court's finding that reunification with either Father or Mother was not attainable within the foreseeable future

relevance.OUT-02: It is the Supreme Court of Maryland's clearest statement that internally inconsistent findings cannot justify withholding termination.
relevance.OUT-03: It holds that indefinite third-party custody is not an acceptable substitute for permanency when reunification is impossible.
relevance.OUT-05: It constrains a juvenile court's power to keep a case open rather than resolve permanency.

cases.citation: No. 1267, Sept. Term 2020 (Md. Ct. Spec. App. July 29, 2021)
cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: The court vacated a CINA adjudication and disposition, holding that at a contested adjudicatory hearing the department must introduce evidence complying with the Maryland Rules, and that findings resting solely on attorney proffers and an unadmitted report are clearly erroneous.
cases.quote: the court's findings of fact at the contested adjudicatory hearing were clearly erroneous because they were based solely on proffers from counsel and the unadmitted Report

relevance.DEC-05: It defines what the department must actually prove, and how, once it files a CINA petition that the parent contests.
relevance.OUT-05: It shows when an adjudication must be undone and the matter reheard rather than allowed to stand.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading recent Maryland reversal for an evidentiarily empty adjudication.

cases.case_name: B.H. v. Anne Arundel County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: The court affirmed an administrative law judge's decision upholding a finding of indicated child abuse, holding that a mixed question of law and fact in such an appeal is reviewed under the substantial evidence test.
cases.quote: When the agency decision being judicially reviewed is a mixed question of law and fact, the reviewing court applies the substantial evidence test.

relevance.DEC-03: It states the standard of review that governs a parent's administrative challenge to an indicated finding under FL § 5-706.1.
relevance.INP-03: The case arose from a joint police and department response to a report of abuse.
relevance.FAIL-01: It shows how deferential judicial review of an agency abuse finding actually is.

cases.case_name: Department of Human Resources v. Cosby
cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: The court held that collateral estoppel may be raised and applied in an FL § 5-706.1 appeal hearing, so an ALJ properly dismissed the appeal of an indicated finding already litigated in the CINA case.
cases.quote: we hold that the doctrine of collateral estoppel may be raised and applied in a F.L. § 5-706.1 hearing

relevance.DEC-03: It controls the preclusive effect of a CINA adjudication on a parent's separate administrative appeal of an indicated finding.
relevance.DEC-01: It sets out the § 5-706.1 notice and hearing scheme that follows indicated and unsubstantiated dispositions alike.
relevance.INP-10: It describes the statutory sequence from investigation through finding, notice, and appeal.

cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: The court held that the juvenile court erred in finding reasonable efforts where the department made only a single vocational referral to address the father's unemployment, because the department's services must address the actual impediments to reunification.
cases.quote: the obligation to render "reasonable efforts" rests on the Department, not the parent

relevance.ACT-02: James G. is Maryland's leading intermediate-appellate statement of what court-ordered reunification services must actually consist of.
relevance.ACT-01: It holds that token or unmatched service referrals do not discharge the agency's obligation.
relevance.OUT-01: It defines the reasonable-efforts predicate that must be satisfied before reunification is abandoned.
relevance.FAIL-03: Reasonable efforts is a Title IV-E funding condition and this case shows what falls below it.
relevance.PMC-01: It supplies a concrete Maryland yardstick for CFSR-style assessment of service adequacy.
relevance.DEC-06: It measures the sufficiency of front-end, non-court services offered to avert deeper intervention.

cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: The court held that appellate jurisdiction under CJP § 12-303(3)(x) is not limited to orders concerning minors, and affirmed the change of a 19-year-old's permanency plan from reunification to another planned permanent living arrangement.
cases.quote: We are unconvinced that the appellate jurisdiction conferred by CJP § 12-303(3)(x) is limited to orders affecting the care and custody of minors.

relevance.OUT-04: This is Maryland's principal published decision on permanency planning for a young adult who remains in foster care past 18.
relevance.ACT-03: It reviews the standards for continuing an out-of-home placement for an older youth.
relevance.FAIL-01: It secures appellate review of permanency orders entered after the youth reaches majority.

cases.citation: No. 1609, Sept. Term 2024 (Md. App. Ct. July 1, 2025)
cases.holding: The court held that in CINA cases a department is generally required under the ADA to make reasonable accommodations for parents with disabilities in providing reunification services, provided the parent makes the disability and needed accommodation known, and affirmed the award of custody and guardianship to the grandparents.
cases.quote: the Department is generally required under the ADA to make reasonable accommodations for parents with disabilities in rendering reunification efforts in CINA cases

relevance.FAIL-05: It is Maryland's most developed treatment of disability discrimination in the delivery of child-welfare services.
relevance.ACT-02: It defines the accommodation component of court-ordered reunification services.
relevance.ACT-01: It allocates to the parent the burden of identifying needed accommodations in voluntary service planning.
relevance.OUT-01: It integrates ADA accommodation into the CINA reasonable-efforts inquiry that governs reunification.
relevance.OUT-03: It affirms custody and guardianship to relatives as the permanency outcome once reunification efforts are exhausted.
relevance.ACT-04: It approves kinship permanency with grandparents coupled with supervised parental visitation.
relevance.DEC-06: It examines the adequacy of front-end services arranged for a disabled parent.

cases.case_name: Freed v. Worcester County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: The court held that parents investigated for neglect have no right to compel the department to disclose the identity of the person who reported them, rejecting due process and equal protection challenges to the confidentiality and good-faith immunity scheme of FL §§ 5-707 and 5-708.
cases.quote: no one has the right to obtain the name of the reporter from Social Services for the purpose of initiating litigation under 42 U.S.C. § 1983

relevance.INP-02: It is the Maryland decision squarely protecting the anonymity of a voluntary, non-mandated reporter.
relevance.INP-06: It upholds the confidentiality that makes anonymous and hotline reporting workable.
relevance.INP-01: It explains the good-faith immunity in FL § 5-708 that underwrites mandated and permissive reporting alike.
relevance.FAIL-06: It sets the boundary between agency confidentiality obligations and a subject's demand for disclosure.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the controlling Maryland authority limiting transparency claims against child-abuse records.
relevance.PMC-03: It explains the legislative policy of confidentiality that any external review mechanism must operate within.
relevance.INP-08: The reporter-confidentiality rule it announces applies to educators and other mandated reporters.

cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: In a suit by an abused child against the State and social workers, the court affirmed dismissal, holding that state personnel retained statutory immunity absent malice or gross negligence, that the tort claim failed for lack of the required notice, and that violation of state-mandated investigative procedures is not itself a federal due process deprivation.
cases.quote: The violation of State-mandated procedures may well give rise to an action under State law, if the appropriate preconditions to such an action are followed

relevance.FAIL-04: It sets out the immunity and notice obstacles a child injured under agency supervision faces in Maryland.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the Maryland decision on remedies for serious injury suffered after the agency failed to act on abuse reports.
relevance.INP-01: It recites the statutory purpose of mandated reporting, immunity, and prompt investigation that frames agency duties.
relevance.PMC-02: It shows that individual litigation is a weak accountability tool, throwing weight onto audit and oversight.
relevance.PMC-04: It is a Maryland serious-injury case illustrating what post hoc review can and cannot achieve.

cases.case_name: Montgomery County Department of Health & Human Services v. P.F.
cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: The court affirmed an order requiring the agency to reclassify a sexual-abuse finding as 'ruled out' and to expunge its records and central registry entry, where the ALJ found no credible evidence that abuse occurred after a deficient investigation.
cases.quote: MCHHS must comply with the order to reclassify the case as "ruled out," and expunge its records and registry.

relevance.DEC-01: It is the leading Maryland case on the 'ruled out' disposition and the expungement it compels.
relevance.DEC-03: It shows that an indicated or unsubstantiated finding can be overturned and stricken when the investigation is unsound.
relevance.OUT-05: It is the administrative analogue of a dismissal, with mandatory record consequences.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a reversal of an agency abuse finding on judicial review.
relevance.FAIL-06: It enforces the agency's affirmative duty to correct and purge its records.
relevance.PMC-05: It establishes a concrete, enforceable expungement remedy against a Maryland child-welfare agency.

cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: The court vacated orders removing reunification from the permanency plan because the juvenile court relied on a polygraph examination, holding that material the department may lawfully use as an investigative tool is not thereby admissible as evidence in an adjudicative proceeding.
cases.quote: we must maintain the careful distinction between an investigative tool and evidence that has sufficient reliability for consideration in an adjudicative proceeding

relevance.DEC-02: It draws the line between what CPS may gather during an investigation and what a court may rely on.
relevance.INP-07: The case began with a hospital report of a two-month-old's unexplained fractures.
relevance.INP-03: It illustrates the joint medical, police and department response to suspected non-accidental trauma.
relevance.INP-10: It shows the escalation from a hospital notification to full investigation and removal.
relevance.INP-12: All three children were placed in shelter care the same day, and the court reviews that emergency action.
relevance.DEC-04: It reviews an emergency removal predicated on medical findings of non-accidental trauma.
relevance.ACT-04: The children were placed with a paternal grandmother rather than in stranger foster care.
relevance.ACT-03: It reviews the placement and permanency consequences of an unexplained-injury removal.
relevance.ACT-05: The arrangement required the parents to vacate the home while grandparents cared for the children.
relevance.ACT-06: The case turns on emergency medical evaluation and skeletal survey findings driving the intervention.
relevance.OUT-06: It addresses proof problems where a child suffers serious injury and the perpetrator cannot be identified.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a reversal for the juvenile court's reliance on inherently unreliable evidence.

cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
cases.holding: The court reversed termination of the parental rights of a mother with a treated mental illness, holding that the juvenile court had to hold a further hearing to evaluate her rehabilitation and the effect of the foster family's withdrawal before deciding the child's best interests.
cases.quote: Because the juvenile court erred in not holding another hearing—not fully evaluating Mother's mental health progress in light of her fundamental right to parent

relevance.FAIL-05: It is the leading recent Maryland case refusing to treat a parent's mental illness as a standing ground for termination.
relevance.OUT-02: It requires current, not stale, evidence of a parent's condition before parental rights are severed.

cases.case_name: Weller v. Department of Social Services for the City of Baltimore
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of most of a father's § 1983 claims against the Baltimore City department but held that his allegation that the State transferred custody of his son on an emergency basis and then denied him any hearing stated a procedural due process claim that could not be dismissed.
cases.quote: Due process does not mandate a prior hearing in cases where emergency action may be needed to protect a child.

relevance.FAIL-02: Weller is the Fourth Circuit's Maryland-based statement of when removal without a prior hearing violates due process.
relevance.DEC-04: It authorizes emergency removal without a pre-deprivation hearing while requiring prompt post-deprivation process.
relevance.INP-12: It defines the constitutional floor for protective custody taken before judicial authorization.
relevance.ACT-03: It ties the lawfulness of a foster placement to prompt judicial ratification of the removal.

cases.case_name: Martin v. Saint Mary's Department of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for Maryland caseworkers on qualified immunity, holding that the record showed at most negligent miscommunication causing an out-of-state removal, and that the mother's due process rights were not violated where a post-deprivation hearing occurred and the children were returned within 24 hours.
cases.quote: Because a § 1983 claim cannot be sustained, it follows that the defendants are entitled to qualified immunity.

relevance.FAIL-02: It is the controlling Fourth Circuit qualified-immunity decision for Maryland caseworkers accused of wrongful removal.
relevance.DEC-04: It addresses the authority of a Maryland department to take temporary custody when it believes a child is in serious, immediate danger.
relevance.INP-12: It confirms the statutory basis in FL § 5-709(c) for emergency protective custody and the process that must follow.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for Maryland officials, holding that investigative home visits by social workers are not measured by criminal-search standards and that the entry of the caseworker and accompanying deputies into a consenting foster mother's home was not unreasonable.
cases.quote: investigative home visits by social workers are not subject to the same scrutiny as searches in the criminal context

relevance.DEC-02: It is the Fourth Circuit's Maryland case on the Fourth Amendment standard for CPS home entry during an investigation.
relevance.INP-03: It addresses the presence of accompanying law enforcement during a social-services home visit.
relevance.FAIL-02: It sets the reasonableness baseline against which an unlawful entry or seizure claim is measured in this circuit.
relevance.INP-12: It supplies the search-and-seizure framework governing protective action taken at the home.

cases.case_name: Hodge ex rel. Hodge v. Jones
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that Maryland's confidential retention of an 'unsubstantiated' and 'ruled out' child-abuse investigation file did not violate the family's constitutional privacy, familial or due process rights, because there was no cognizable stigma and no loss of a tangible interest.
cases.quote: a conclusory allegation of reputational injury which, absent a cognizable stigma and the ensuing loss of a tangible interest, fails to state a cause of action under Sec. 1983

relevance.DEC-01: It governs what the agency may keep on file after a report is ruled out or unsubstantiated.
relevance.DEC-03: It defines the constitutional limits on challenging record retention following an abuse investigation.
relevance.INP-02: It confirms that a mistaken report absorbed into a confidential file creates no federal claim.
relevance.INP-06: It upholds the confidentiality regime surrounding intake records.
relevance.INP-09: It describes the statutory and regulatory record-keeping scheme that oversight bodies must work within.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the leading Fourth Circuit case on Maryland child-abuse record confidentiality and expungement demands.
relevance.PMC-05: It marks the constitutional ceiling on transparency and expungement claims against Maryland's child-welfare records.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of Rule 60(b)(5) relief from, and the entry of a modified, consent decree governing Baltimore City's foster care system, holding that the State had not shown that the law-of-the-case finding of a private right of action under 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(16) was overruled or clearly wrong.
cases.quote: we do not now hold that § 671(a)(16) provides a private right of action

relevance.FAIL-03: It is the operative federal decision keeping Baltimore City's foster care system under judicial supervision for Title IV-E case-plan failures.
relevance.PMC-01: It shows how federal case-plan and case-review requirements are enforced against a Maryland agency outside the CFSR process.
relevance.PMC-02: Long-running institutional litigation is the principal external audit mechanism for Maryland's largest child-welfare agency.
relevance.PMC-03: It illustrates the external-review function that citizen panels are meant to serve.
relevance.PMC-06: The decree and its modifications are the richest public dataset on systemic Maryland foster care deficiencies.
relevance.INP-09: Court-supervised systemic monitoring here functions as the oversight trigger for agency practice change.
relevance.OUT-04: The decree's case-plan and case-review obligations reach older youth preparing to leave care.

cases.case_name: Wolf v. Fauquier County Board of Supervisors
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for social services defendants, holding that a parent who complained that a child-abuse investigation was mishandled and unduly prolonged could not show that the investigation fell below the minimum notice-and-opportunity-to-be-heard standards procedural due process requires.
cases.quote: she cannot show that the investigation did not meet the minimum standards required by procedural due process

relevance.DEC-02: It is the Fourth Circuit's statement of the (low) constitutional floor for the conduct of a CPS investigation.
relevance.INP-05: It addresses a parent's own demands on the agency during an investigation she initiated contact about.
relevance.INP-10: It describes what process is due as a screening becomes a full investigation.
relevance.ACT-05: It involves a protective order obtained in the course of the agency's intervention.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a State may terminate parental rights, and left to the States the choice of any standard equal to or higher than that.
cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

relevance.OUT-02: Santosky is the federal constitutional floor that Maryland's clear-and-convincing TPR standard implements.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that a state agency's failure to protect a child from a known risk of parental abuse, where the child remained in his father's custody, did not deprive him of liberty in violation of the Due Process Clause.
cases.quote: The Clause is phrased as a limitation on the State's power to act, not as a guarantee of certain minimal levels of safety and security.

relevance.OUT-06: DeShaney is the reason that fatality and serious-injury claims against Maryland agencies proceed in state tort law rather than under § 1983.
relevance.FAIL-04: It forecloses the federal substantive due process theory for a death occurring while the child is in parental custody.
relevance.FAIL-02: It marks the constitutional asymmetry between wrongful removal (actionable) and failure to remove (generally not).
relevance.PMC-04: It explains why fatality accountability in the United States is legislative and administrative rather than constitutional.

cases.case_name: McClanahan v. Washington County Department of Social Services
cases.holding: Reversing the Court of Special Appeals and remanding to the ALJ, the Court held that a person may be placed on the DHR central registry as responsible for child abuse — including abuse by mental injury — only if the person intended to injure the child or acted in reckless disregard of the child's welfare.
cases.quote: inclusion on the central registry as a child abuser is not permitted unless Mother intended to harm R or acted in reckless disregard of R's welfare

relevance.DEC-03: It supplies the scienter element Maryland requires before an agency may make an indicated abuse finding, and it corrects the contrary intermediate-appellate rule the earlier brief relied on.
relevance.DEC-01: It means that conduct that was neither intended to injure nor reckless cannot support an indicated finding, so such reports must end in an unsubstantiated or ruled-out disposition.

cases.case_name: Taylor v. Harford County Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Court vacated an ALJ's finding of 'indicated' child physical abuse, holding that the ALJ erred by using tort foreseeability to infer intent and that an intentional act causing unintended injury supports an indicated finding only if the act was reckless or deliberately intended to harm the child.
cases.quote: We hold that, under the circumstances here present, the intentional act must be shown to have been either reckless in its nature or deliberately intended to harm the child

relevance.DEC-03: Taylor is the Court of Appeals' controlling decision on what an agency must establish to sustain an 'indicated' child abuse finding, and it is the source of the scienter rule McClanahan later extended.
relevance.DEC-01: It construes the COMAR 'ruled out' criterion excluding injury that was accidental or unintentional and not reckless or deliberate.

cases.holding: Affirming the change of four children's permanency plans from reunification to adoption, the Court held that the reasonable-efforts requirement is case-specific and must be measured against the services actually at the department's disposal, so efforts were reasonable where the department made and pursued referrals but funding-dependent services never became available to a developmentally disabled mother.
cases.quote: We shall hold that the "reasonable efforts" requirement is case-specific, and must be considered in light of the services at the Department's disposal.

relevance.ACT-02: It is the Court of Appeals' controlling statement of how much the department must do to satisfy its court-ordered reunification-services obligation.
relevance.ACT-01: It measures the department's referrals to voluntary services against the specific impediments to reunification identified for this family.
relevance.OUT-01: It defines the reasonable-efforts predicate that must be satisfied before reunification ceases to be the plan.
relevance.FAIL-05: It addresses what a department owes a developmentally disabled parent when the specialized services she needs are unavailable.
relevance.FAIL-03: Reasonable efforts is a Title IV-E funding condition, and this case sets the Maryland high-court benchmark for judging compliance.
relevance.DEC-06: It assesses the adequacy of front-end and non-court services arranged to avert the deeper intervention that followed.

cases.holding: The Court reversed a grandparent-visitation order and overruled contrary prior decisions, holding that Maryland's grandparent visitation statute may be applied constitutionally only after a threshold finding of parental unfitness or exceptional circumstances showing current or future detriment to the child from the absence of visitation, before any best-interest analysis.
cases.quote: there must be a finding of either parental unfitness or exceptional circumstances demonstrating the current or future detriment to the child, absent visitation from his or her grandparents

relevance.ACT-04: It is the source of the threshold showing a relative or other third party must make before a court may order contact with a child over a parent's objection.
relevance.OUT-03: It fixes the constitutional predicate a kinship caregiver must satisfy before a court may order a third-party access arrangement as part of permanency.

cases.holding: The Court reversed an award of custody to maternal grandparents, holding that in a private custody dispute between a fit natural parent and third parties the court may not reach the best-interest test unless it first finds both parents unfit or extraordinary circumstances significantly detrimental to the child's remaining in parental custody.
cases.quote: in private custody actions involving private third-parties where the parents are fit, absent extraordinary (i.e., exceptional) circumstances, the constitutional right is the ultimate determinative factor

relevance.OUT-03: It is the Maryland decision establishing the parental presumption that governs any third-party custody or guardianship permanency arrangement, and the authority Ta'Niya C. and Victoria C. are reconciling.

cases.holding: Reversing the Court of Special Appeals, the Court held that an order amending a permanency plan from reunification to foster care or adoption, although interlocutory, is immediately appealable under CJP § 12-303(3)(x) as an order changing the terms of a parent's care and custody.
cases.quote: We hold that an order amending a permanency plan calling for reunification to foster care or adoption is immediately appealable.

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the jurisdictional predicate for every Maryland appeal from a permanency-plan order, including the appeals in Yve S. and Andre J.
relevance.ACT-03: It establishes that a parent may obtain immediate appellate review when the plan for a child in out-of-home placement shifts away from reunification.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed a CINA adjudication entered on stipulated facts, holding that a parent's right to a contested CINA adjudicatory hearing is not among the rights requiring a personal, knowing, intelligent and voluntary waiver, and that counsel's concurrence in the stipulated facts in the petition waived it.
cases.quote: Ms. H.'s waiver of a contested CINA adjudicatory hearing was sufficient when her attorney concurred with the stipulated facts.

relevance.DEC-05: It governs what happens procedurally once a department files a CINA petition, and in particular the effect of a parent's counsel agreeing to the facts alleged in it.

cases.holding: Reversing the Court of Special Appeals, the Court held that a mother could maintain an interlocutory appeal from the order awarding temporary custody of her CINA child to the father under departmental supervision, and that subsequent review-hearing orders that changed nothing did not render the appeal moot.
cases.quote: We shall hold that Petitioner had a right to an interlocutory appeal and that the appeal has not been rendered moot by orders issued at subsequent review hearings.

relevance.FAIL-01: It preserves a parent's ability to obtain appellate correction of a CINA custody order despite the churn of periodic review hearings.
relevance.INP-12: It traces the Maryland sequence from emergency shelter care through CINA adjudication to custody orders, and secures review of the order that follows emergency action.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed rejection of facial and as-applied challenges to Virginia's 72-hour emergency-removal statute, holding that a 65-hour weekend delay in judicial review of a protective removal did not violate due process, while reversing dismissal of the parents' § 1983 claim against the county and its social services department arising from the removal itself.
cases.quote: we conclude that section 63.1-248.9, as it was applied in this case so as to permit such a delay, does not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment

relevance.FAIL-02: It is the Fourth Circuit's principal emergency-removal decision and the one the Martin majority relies on when measuring a wrongful-removal claim.
relevance.INP-12: It fixes how long protective custody may last before judicial review without offending due process in this circuit.
relevance.DEC-04: It defines the exigency and post-deprivation-process conditions under which a caseworker may remove a child before any court order.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption/Guardianship of Cadence B.
cases.holding: The Court affirmed a change of permanency plan from reunification to open adoption, holding that the juvenile court did not abuse its discretion in ending reunification efforts where the father had willfully absented himself from meaningful contact and the child was bonded to caregivers willing to provide a permanent home.
cases.quote: if there are weighty circumstances indicating that reunification with the parent is not in the child's best interest, the court should modify the permanency plan to a more appropriate arrangement

relevance.OUT-01: It states when the statutory presumption favoring reunification is overcome and the reunification track may properly be abandoned.

cases.holding: Overruling Janice M. v. Margaret K., the Court held that de facto parenthood is a viable basis for standing to contest custody or visitation and that a de facto parent, unlike other third parties, need not show parental unfitness or exceptional circumstances before the court applies the best-interest standard.
cases.quote: We hold that de facto parenthood is a viable means to establish standing to contest custody or visitation

relevance.ACT-04: It identifies the one category of non-biological caregiver — the de facto parent — who may seek custody or access without carrying the Koshko third-party threshold burden.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed a Mississippi adoption decree, holding that 'domicile' under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law, that children born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were themselves domiciled on the reservation, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a).
cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

relevance.INP-11: It is the controlling federal decision on when an Indian child's case belongs exclusively to a tribal court, the jurisdictional question Maryland's sole ICWA decision leaves undecided.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed the Seventh Circuit, holding that the 'reasonable efforts' requirement of 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15) confers no federally enforceable right on foster children or their parents, whether through § 1983 or an implied right of action, and is instead enforced by the Secretary through plan approval.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.FAIL-03: It is the Supreme Court's statement of how Title IV-E compliance failures are and are not enforceable, the federal backdrop against which the Baltimore City consent decree in L.J. v. Wilbon operates.
relevance.PMC-01: It explains why federal monitoring (CFSR and the Secretary's plan-approval process), rather than private suit, is the mechanism for policing state reasonable-efforts performance.

cases.holding: The Court held that a juvenile court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction to direct how a local department, once appointed by the SSA as a foster child's representative payee, allocates the child's OASDI benefits, but required the department to notify the child's counsel when it applies to be payee and of the benefits it receives.
cases.quote: a local department of social services need not seek permission from a juvenile court in order to exercise its statutory and regulatory-guided discretion as a duly appointed representative payee

relevance.OUT-04: It governs the survivor's and disability benefits belonging to a youth in long-term foster care, resources that matter most when the youth is preparing to transition out of care.
relevance.PMC-02: It is the Maryland decision on a department's use of a foster child's federal benefits to reimburse itself for the cost of his care, and on the notice that makes that practice auditable.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API in this session and its opinion text read; all quotes were machine-verified as exact substrings of the retrieved majority-opinion text after whitespace and curly-quote normalization. No unpublished or memorandum decisions were used.

Court naming: Maryland renamed its courts in December 2022. CourtListener court_id 'md' is the Court of Appeals of Maryland (now the Supreme Court of Maryland) and 'mdctspecapp' is the Court of Special Appeals of Maryland (now the Appellate Court of Maryland). The 'court' field gives the name the court bore on the decision date; the court_id is unchanged.

CourtListener date_filed anomalies: for Lassiter (cluster 110506) CourtListener reports 1981-08-28 and for Baltimore City DSS v. Bouknight (cluster 112360) it reports 1989-10-02. These appear to be term/docket dates rather than the opinion dates. The date_decided fields above report the CourtListener cluster value verbatim; the reporter citations (452 U.S. 18 (1981); 493 U.S. 549 (1990)) control, and the 'year' fields follow the reporter. Verify against the U.S. Reports before filing anything that turns on the date.

Slip-form citations are used for three clusters that carry no reporter citation in CourtListener: In re M.H. (cluster 5313734), In re M.Z. (cluster 10362660) and In re Z.F. & B.F. (cluster 10621099). In re M.H. is in fact reported at 252 Md. App. 29 (as cited in the Supreme Court of Maryland's opinion in In re T.K.), but the cluster record lacks that citation, so slip form was used per the citation rule.

ICWA / state ICWA: Maryland has exactly one high-court published ICWA decision, In re Nicole B., 410 Md. 33 (2009), addressing 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) 'active efforts.' The Court of Special Appeals decision below (In re Nicole B., 175 Md. App. 450 (2007)) was retrieved but is NOT included because the Court of Appeals reversed it. No published Maryland appellate decision was found on ICWA qualified expert witnesses, placement preferences, or transfer to tribal jurisdiction; on the transfer point, In re Nicole B. recites without deciding the circuit court's denial of the Yankton Sioux Tribe's transfer motion as untimely. Maryland has no state ICWA statute. For those sub-issues practitioners must rely on 25 U.S.C. §§ 1911-1915 and the 2016 BIA regulations directly.

Extended foster care / jurisdiction past 18: In re Andre J., 223 Md. App. 305 (2015), is the only published Maryland appellate decision found addressing permanency planning for a youth who has passed 18 and remains in care (APPLA for a 19-year-old), and it holds that CJP § 12-303(3)(x) appellate jurisdiction is not limited to minors. No published Maryland decision was found construing the voluntary placement agreement / re-entry provisions of Maryland's extended foster care program to age 21. OUT-04 is therefore supported by Andre J., In re M.Z. (right to contest closure of a CINA case) and L.J. v. Wilbon (federal case-plan and case-review obligations), and remains the thinnest node in this jurisdiction.

Differential response / alternative response (DEC-06) and citizen review panels (PMC-03): no Maryland appellate decision on point was located. DEC-06 is mapped to the closest available authority on the adequacy of pre-petition and non-court services (In re Shirley B., In re James G., In re Z.F. & B.F.). PMC-03 is mapped to the external-oversight authorities (L.J. v. Wilbon, Horridge, Freed); CAPTA § 5106a(c) itself is the operative requirement and no case enforces it.

Educational disclosure (INP-08) and self-report/guardian request (INP-05): no Maryland appellate decision turns on educator reporting or a guardian's request for voluntary help as such. These nodes are mapped to the general mandated-reporting duty and reporter-immunity/confidentiality authorities (Horridge, Freed) plus fact-adjacent cases (In re Shirley B., In re Priscilla B., Wolf). Md. Code, Fam. Law §§ 5-704, 5-705 and 5-708 remain the primary authority.

§ 1983 / Fourth Circuit: Jordan by Jordan v. Jackson, 15 F.3d 333 (4th Cir. 1994) — the circuit's principal emergency-removal / post-deprivation-hearing decision, cited by the Martin majority — could not be retrieved through the CourtListener search API in this session and is therefore NOT included. Practitioners should read it alongside Weller and Martin. Wolf v. Fauquier County is a Virginia case; it is included because it is published Fourth Circuit precedent binding in Maryland on the due process floor for CPS investigations.

Maryland state-law liability for a child's death or serious injury under agency supervision runs through Horridge v. St. Mary's County DSS (duty to the identified child; public duty doctrine inapplicable) and Wells v. State (Maryland Tort Claims Act notice; statutory immunity absent malice or gross negligence). DeShaney forecloses the parallel federal substantive due process theory where the child was in parental, not state, custody. No Maryland appellate decision was found on children who go missing from foster care.

Central registry / due process (DEC-03): the FL § 5-706.1 appeal scheme is the operative mechanism. B.H. (substantial-evidence review), McClanahan (no scienter element for mental injury), Cosby (collateral estoppel available) and P.F. (reclassification to 'ruled out' plus mandatory expungement) together map the contested-case path. Hodge v. Jones supplies the federal ceiling on record-retention challenges.

Two quotes required judgment calls a reviewer should check. (1) In re Z.F. & B.F.: the full holding sentence exceeds the 30-word limit; the quote used preserves the qualifier 'generally' but the opinion's condition — the parent must make the disability and the needed accommodation known to the department — appears only in the holding field. (2) In re Jayden G.: the 12-word quote states the discretion rule; the accompanying holding supplies the disposition. Read both opinions in full before relying on them.

The pre-existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the MD node files are keyword-matched noise (e.g. 'In re Petition of Featherfall Restoration', 'In re: Foster Farm', 'Doe v. Catholic Relief Services'). None survived verification; none is carried forward. This brief replaces them entirely.
API usage: approximately 65 CourtListener requests, paced at one every two seconds, well within the 150-request budget. No repo files were modified.

The brief currently states Maryland's scienter rule backwards.

Absent entirely from DEC-03.

The brief concedes it could not retrieve it; it is on CourtListener (clusters 661725 and 7027839) and is required reading alongside Weller and Martin for FAIL-02, INP-12 and DEC-04.

Washington County Department of Social Services, 445 Md. 691 (2015), for DEC-03 and DEC-01: it is the Court of Appeals' controlling scienter rule for the central registry — intent to injure or reckless disregard — and it reversed the intermediate opinion whose contrary rule the prior brief had adopted, so the DEC-03 statement of Maryland law is now corrected.

Added Taylor v. Harford County Department of Social Services, 384 Md. 213 (2004), for DEC-03 and DEC-01: it is the high-court source of the reckless-or-deliberate requirement for an 'indicated' finding and of the 'ruled out' criterion for accidental, non-reckless injury, and it is the decision McClanahan extends to mental injury.

Added In re Shirley B., 419 Md. 1 (2011), for ACT-01, ACT-02, OUT-01, DEC-06, FAIL-03 and FAIL-05: it is the Court of Appeals' affirmance in the case the prior brief cited only at 191 Md. App. 678, and it states the controlling case-specific reasonable-efforts standard measured by the services at the department's disposal.

Added Koshko v. Haining, 398 Md. 404 (2007), for ACT-04 and OUT-03: the brief repeatedly invoked 'the Koshko threshold' through Victoria C. without ever citing the decision that created it; Koshko supplies the parental-unfitness-or-exceptional-circumstances prerequisite for any third-party access order.

Added McDermott v. Dougherty, 385 Md. 320 (2005), for OUT-03: it is the parental-presumption decision in third-party custody disputes, including the 'constitutional right is the ultimate determinative factor' formulation, which Ta'Niya C., Koshko and Victoria C. are all arguing about. It is mapped to OUT-03 rather than OUT-02 because it is a custody, not a termination, case and H.W. holds that custody factors have no place in a TPR analysis.

Added In re Damon M., 362 Md. 429 (2001), for FAIL-01 and ACT-03: it holds permanency-plan amendment orders immediately appealable under CJP § 12-303(3)(x), the jurisdictional predicate on which Yve S., Andre J. and In re C.E. all rest.

Added In re Blessen H., 392 Md. 684 (2006), for DEC-05: it governs the effect of a parent's counsel stipulating to the facts of a CINA petition and holds that a contested adjudicatory hearing is not a right requiring personal knowing and intelligent waiver.

Added In re Joseph N., 407 Md. 278 (2009), for FAIL-01 and INP-12: it preserves interlocutory review of a CINA custody order entered after emergency shelter care and holds later review-hearing orders do not moot the appeal. NOTE: the verifier described it as a decision on shelter care itself; the opinion is in fact an appealability and mootness decision arising out of an emergency shelter-care sequence, and the relevance sentences are written to that narrower holding.

Added Jordan v. Jackson, 15 F.3d 333 (4th Cir. 1994) (cluster 661725), for FAIL-02, INP-12 and DEC-04: the prior brief conceded it could not retrieve this case; it was retrieved and read in this session. Fauquier County it arises in Virginia but is published Fourth Circuit precedent binding in Maryland, and it supplies the circuit's rule on how long protective custody may precede judicial review.

Added In re Adoption/Guardianship of Cadence B., 417 Md. 146 (2010), for OUT-01: it states when the presumption favoring reunification is overcome and the plan may properly change to adoption. CORRECTION: the verifier described Cadence B. as a decision on a parent's participation and representation in a TPR proceeding and as the Maryland counterpart to Lassiter. The retrieved opinion is not that case — it is a permanency-plan-change appeal decided on abuse-of-discretion review, and it is mapped accordingly. Added Conover v. Conover, 450 Md. 51 (2016), for ACT-04: it recognizes de facto parenthood and exempts a de facto parent from the Koshko third-party threshold, which defines the outer boundary of who may seek custody or access to a child in or leaving care.

Added Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989), for INP-11: INP-11 previously rested on a single Maryland case (In re Nicole B.) that addresses only ICWA 'active efforts.' Maryland has no published appellate decision on tribal jurisdiction, transfer, or placement preferences, so the node is completed with the controlling U.S. Supreme Court decision on exclusive tribal jurisdiction and federal-law domicile under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a). This is the federal standard, mapped because no state authority exists on the point.

Added Suter v. Artist M., 503 U.S. 347 (1992), for FAIL-03 and PMC-01: both nodes previously rested on L.J. v. Wilbon alone. Suter is the controlling U.S. Supreme Court decision holding the Title IV-E 'reasonable efforts' condition privately unenforceable and committing compliance to the Secretary — the federal standard against which CFSR monitoring and the Baltimore City consent decree both operate. Mapped as the federal standard because no Maryland decision addresses IV-E enforcement.

Added In re Ryan W., 434 Md. 577 (2013), for OUT-04 and PMC-02: it is the Court of Appeals decision on a Maryland department's use of a foster child's Social Security survivor's benefits to reimburse itself for the cost of his care, on the juvenile court's lack of jurisdiction over that allocation, and on the notice owed to the child's counsel — the closest Maryland authority to a financial-accountability audit of agency practice, and directly relevant to the resources of a youth transitioning out of care.
